top5.why: C14 has 130 major episodes, 3.5x the next candidate, and ~119 remain after the ~864 templated catalogue PRs are removed, so the lead is not volume. Those majors are incident, data-correctness, billing and security fixes on the pipeline every warehouse customer shares (#110610 and #113196 at P=16.0, #114623, #125154). On top of that he merged a credentials service and integrations SDK and migrated call sites in 21 products (#124844, #125029). The self-inflicted credential outage (#86546 -> #122385) and thin human review on ~1,200 PRs lower confidence but do not change the order.

C07 builds shared mechanisms and migrates callers himself: posthog/ingress ended silent webhook loss for at least eight providers (#100292, #101508), and one ownership reader replaced four separate ones (#103852, P=16.0). He also reversed a production regression that had tripled web-analytics dashboard latency (#104208) and cut fresh migrations from ~20 to ~5 minutes for every CI shard (#91646). His record is among the cleanest at high volume (0.983, 0 reverts) and his 24 change requests on others' PRs were 95% adopted, the strongest corrective review signal in the pool.

C11 changed paths every user and every request goes through: the boot document fell from 544KB to 10KB and 1.1-1.6 MiB of eager JS per scene came off the critical path (#94059), with a CI ratchet to hold the gain (#126768). He also fixed a production OAuth incident (#83929), integration-token loss (#108163, P=16.0) and six access-control leaks (#102477). His quality is below median (0.952, 13 follow-ups), but none touched a major PR and his latest repo-wide ORM change (#126463) is too new to judge, which is why he sits below C07.

C04 is PostHog's de facto OAuth/MCP security owner: 13 of his 26 majors close account-takeover, privilege-escalation or cross-customer leak paths (#113013, #113014, #105547 at P=13.0, #127775). He also built the step-up scope flow and MCP tool catalog that let agents use PostHog safely (#127702, #125197). Structurally he is the top bridge in the review graph (0.0792, 12 communities) with 16 requesters, and the security team routes its auth PRs to him. His quality rate (0.945) and single-reviewer concentration are the reasons he is not higher.

Feature-flags engineer who single-handedly drove the flag_evaluations storage migration end to end (ingestion, ClickHouse, HogQL, data deletion, cohorts, CDP) while serving as the main approver for the feature-flags and experiments teams.

next5.why: C18 hardened the layers every team builds on: one access-precedence resolver (#114423, P=16.0), closed privilege escalations (#105467, #122926), and DNS-rebinding defences applied to every host-taking warehouse source by default (#101362). In three days he removed compromised eMudhra roots from every runtime PostHog ships (#121580, #121626, #122294), and he moved the app to an enforced CSP on signed-in, shared and embedded pages (#106238, #116719). His 37 major episodes are 2nd of 22, although his review weight is low and the CSP rollout needed ~24 repair PRs.

Data-correctness engineer for PostHog's persons store and capture ingestion: he owns the deletion, deduplication and Postgres/ClickHouse consistency machinery for person data, and the capture rate limiter, shipping a long series of fixes in core pipelines that every product reads from.
Lead builder of Replay Vision (AI analysis of session recordings): he authors 76% of the area's PRs and also owns its billing, privacy and rasterizer plumbing, with an unusually clean quality record.

The highest-volume builder on the Workflows/Messaging product, who in October drove the migration of PostHog's own transactional email (password resets, invites, alerts) off Customer.io onto Workflows, while also hardening the CDP job queue and realtime cohorts that every workflow depends on.

Leading builder of PostHog's cloud agent Tasks product (PostHog Code / Desktop cloud runs): he owns the sandbox lifecycle, run reliability and the agent side of the LLM gateway, and is the top author in Product: Tasks among 58 authors.

context_summary.primary: PostHog's leverage this window sat in the correctness of its data-ingestion paths more than in new feature surface. Product: Warehouse sources holds 15.2% of major episodes (`area[Product: Warehouse sources].major_share`), but its 18.7% PR share is inflated by ~864 templated add-source/table PRs, and its two leading authors (C14, 87.7% of his work there; C01, 93.8%) carry 130 and 32 major episodes, so the area reads as two people's output rather than a company-wide theme; changelog counts mislead in the same way, because one '44 new MCP tools' entry is counted in many areas. The densest important work is where the changelog barely looks: Django platform has 10.9% of major episodes on 4.4% of PRs (`area[Django platform (API/models/auth)]`), and the three ingestion areas (nodejs CDP 8.4%, rust 2.9%, personhog 1.9%) hold 13.2% of major work with zero changelog entries, which is where C09, C20, C16 and C05 fixed silent data loss. The second priority was securing the identity and credential surface as AI agents connect to PostHog: C04 (13 security majors), C18 (37 major episodes), C19, C09, C11 and C01 all closed auth, OAuth/MCP or credential-leak holes, and C14's credentials service moved integration secrets for 21 products (#124844, #125029). Structurally, community 1 (purity 0.176) holds seven candidates, the devex, security and frontend-platform core, and four of the top bridges (C04 0.0792, C22 0.0776, C11 0.0556, C12 0.0418); no area has a single point of approval, but the largest stream has one at person level: C15 reviewed 778 and C01 205 of C14's PRs, and 46 of C01's 76 majors had only bot approval. Because 40% of human-authored PRs were approved only by an AI bot (audit note 6), I weighted post-merge behaviour (reverts, follow-up fixes, self-repair chains) and the criticality of specific PRs above first-pass rates and approval centrality.
context_summary.second: Warehouse sources looks like the centre of gravity (`area[Product: Warehouse sources].prs_share` 18.7%, 15.2% of major episodes, 46 changelog entries), but much of that is templated catalogue growth (~864 add-source/table PRs from C14, changelog lines such as '161 new source tables'); the lasting leverage there is the shared sync pipeline and the credentials service (#110610, #124844), not the catalogue count. The quarter's dominant critical theme is security hardening of identity and data boundaries as PostHog opens itself to AI agents: Django platform (API/models/auth) carries 10.9% of major episodes on only 4.4% of PRs, and at least six candidates spent a large share of their major work on auth, secrets or tenant isolation (C18 #114423, C04 #113013, C19 #84698, C09 #109384, C11 #102477, C02 #125069), while MCP tooling appears across many areas' changelogs. The second lever is invisible correctness in core pipelines: Ingestion pipeline & CDP holds 8.4% of major episodes with 0 changelog entries, so the work of C05, C16, C20 and C09 (persons consistency, flag_evaluations, CDP queues) never shows up as features but protects every product's numbers. Structurally, the script finds no area-level single approver (`single_points` = []), yet the biggest stream has one: C15 approved 778 of C14's PRs at a 0.18 h median with no blocking review after 2026-08-04, and review elsewhere runs in closed pairs (C07/C12/C22, C09/C20, C04/C19, C13 with one partner). Bridge scores (C04 0.0792, C22 0.0776, C14 0.0746) mix two kinds of connection, approving across communities (C22, C21) and owning code others touch (C14, C11); I weight the second more. With 40% of human-authored PRs approved only by an AI bot, review-based quality signals are weak across the board, so I lean on post-merge outcomes and self-repair chains.

gates.a: ≥2 major or ≥1 landmark or team leverage top 3
gates.b: <3 reverts and not (follow-up-fix rate ≥8% and in worst 20%)
gates.c: in the top 7 of both independent decisions (else manager justification)

method_notes.sensitivity_scope: reference-weight sensitivity of R only; does not measure sampling, attribution or judge variance

devil.objection: Weak objection: the strongest case is that his lead is partly unreviewed volume. About 32% of his 2,939 PRs are templated add-source/table or GA flips, and only 1,365 carry any recorded review, so roughly 1,200 merged with no review on record. The rest leans on one fast approver: C15 approved 778 of his PRs, with no blocking review after 2026-08-04. Peers follow-up-fixed 31 PRs, 9 of them major. His own fail-closed change #86546 caused a two-hour fleet-wide credential outage, which he reversed in #122385, a self-repair chain. Most of the credentials-service work (#120995, #124844, #125029) merged near or after 2026-10-20, so it has no quality signal yet, and the 21-product migration shows merged call sites, not rollout. The team columns are mid-pack: requested_by 8 (P62), 269 approvals against 1 changes-requested. Even so, ~119 major episodes remain after the template discount, 3.2x the next candidate, so this does not unseat him.
devil.replacement_reason: C17 has the cleaner per-PR record (quality_rate 0.993, P90, vs 0.986; 1 peer follow-up fix vs 31) and the strongest explicit review demand in the pool (requested_by 20, P100, vs 8), on billing and privacy majors such as #86160, #101932 and #101472.
devil.rebuttal: Kept without a re-test: the objection rates itself weak. His 130 major+ episodes are 3.5x the next candidate (37), and about 119 remain after removing roughly 864 templated catalogue PRs. Both independent decisions ranked him #1. The templated share and the AI-only approval share (101 of 211 major PRs) are disclosed as caveats.

devil.objection: His rank leans on network centrality and internal tooling. trust_rank P100 measures approval-network centrality, not being the most trusted approver, and much of it comes from a closed devex loop: C12 or C22 reviewed 261 of his 341 reviewed PRs, and 64% were seen by nobody else. Another 218 of 559 PRs have no recorded human review, which fits bot approval through Stamphog, a tool he owns (not verified). By audit note 6, his 0.997 first-pass rate is therefore not comparable with other candidates'. 176 PRs went to internal AI review tools (ws2-ws4) with only 6 majors and 5 deep reads. Deep-read Q averages 1.5, with Q=1 on the granian pin #104208 and the migration squash #91646, and 61% of diffs were truncated. The platform-wide 1000-row API cap #126411 (Q=1) merged after 2026-10-20 and has no quality signal yet. None of his work is landmark tier. He has 31 major episodes, fewer than C18 (37), C01 and C05 (32).
devil.replacement_reason: C16 is nearly level on the core columns (28 vs 31 major episodes, quality_rate 0.980 vs 0.983) and has more explicit review demand (requested_by 15 vs 11), but his majors are customer-facing data correctness: the flag_evaluations migration across ingestion, HogQL, deletion and CDP (#124397, #117395, #110254) and CDP event-loss fixes (#121819), not internal developer tooling.
devil.rebuttal: Tested: C07 beat the proposed replacement C16 (haacked) in both presentation orders (delivery 1,106 vs 697; shared mechanisms such as the common webhook transport used by many teams). trust_rank is shown with its literal meaning (approval-network centrality), and the closed review loop on his own PRs is disclosed. Both decisions ranked him #2.
